lessons.title: Cash Conversion, Reinvestment Rate, and the Growth Runway

body.text: A moat that generates cash and can redeploy it at the same high returns is a compounding machine. A moat that generates cash with nowhere good to put it is a dividend cheque. Both are fine. Paying compounder prices for the second one is not.

children.text: You now know how to spot a high-return business and test its pricing power. This lesson covers the three questions that decide what those returns are actually worth to you: does the profit turn into cash, how much of that cash can be reinvested, and is there anywhere worthwhile to invest it?
Question 1: Does Profit Become Cash?

markDefs.definition: The share of reported profit that turns into actual operating cash. Commonly measured as cash from operating activities divided by net profit, or as operating cash flow divided by EBITDA.

children.text: Reported profit is an accounting opinion. Cash is a fact. The simplest check is
cash conversion
: compare cash from operating activities in the cash flow statement with net profit in the profit and loss statement, over several years together rather than one year at a time.

body.caption: Compare the five-year totals, since any single year can be distorted by working capital swings

body.title: Illustrative: Profit Rising, Cash Flat (₹ crore)

children.text: Net profit more than doubles from ₹100 crore to ₹210 crore while operating cash goes nowhere, ending at ₹96 crore. Over the five years the company reported ₹750 crore of profit and collected ₹494 crore of cash, a conversion of about 66%. The profits are real on paper and stuck somewhere on the balance sheet: in receivables the company has not collected, or inventory it has not sold.

body.text: This divergence is the single most useful red flag in Indian small and mid caps. When profit grows and operating cash does not, check debtor days and inventory days on Screener.in. If both are climbing, the company may be selling on generous credit or stuffing the distribution channel to report growth. A genuine moat business rarely needs to do either.

children.text: Question 2: The Working Capital Cycle

markDefs.definition: Inventory days plus debtor days minus payable days. It measures how many days of cash are locked in working capital. A negative cycle means suppliers and customers effectively fund the business.

children.text: How long a company's cash stays tied up between paying suppliers and collecting from customers is its
cash conversion cycle
. Screener.in shows this directly in the Ratios section, along with its components.

body.title: What the cycle tells you about power in the value chain

columns.label: Negative or very short cycle
points: Customers pay at or before delivery, and suppliers wait
Growth funds itself, needing little extra capital
Common in branded consumer businesses and quick-selling retail
Often a sign of strength over both suppliers and distributors
Boosts ROCE because capital employed stays small

columns.label: Long or lengthening cycle
points: The company finances customers and holds heavy stock
Every rupee of growth needs extra working capital
Common in project businesses and companies selling to large buyers
Lengthening usually signals weakening bargaining power
Drags ROCE down as capital employed swells

body.title: Calculate the Cycle
body.prompt: A company has inventory days of 45, debtor days of 30, and payable days of 90. What is its cash conversion cycle, in days?
body.explanation: 45 + 30 − 90 = −15 days. The cycle is negative, meaning the company collects from customers about 15 days before it pays suppliers. Its suppliers are effectively funding its working capital, which is why such businesses can grow without raising much capital.

children.text: Question 3: Where Does the Cash Go?

markDefs.definition: The proportion of after-tax operating profit that a company puts back into the business through capital expenditure and additional working capital, rather than paying out.

children.text: A company can do four things with the cash it generates: reinvest in the business, pay dividends, buy back shares, or acquire other companies. The share it puts back into the business is its
reinvestment rate
, and it drives how fast earnings can grow.

body.caption: The same relationship from Chapter 1, now with the return that actually matters: the return on new money

children.text: The Test That Matters Most: Incremental ROCE

markDefs.definition: The return earned on newly invested capital: the change in EBIT over a period divided by the change in capital employed over the same period. It shows whether fresh investment is as profitable as the existing business.

children.text: Historical ROCE tells you what past capital earns.
Incremental ROCE
tells you what new capital earns, which is what determines future growth. Measure it over five years to smooth out lumpy investments.

stats.label: Verdict
stats.context: New capital earns roughly what old capital earns

body.title: Calculate Incremental ROCE
body.prompt: A company's EBIT rose from ₹300 crore in FY20 to ₹420 crore in FY25. Over the same period, capital employed rose from ₹1,500 crore to ₹2,700 crore. What is its incremental ROCE?
body.explanation: Change in EBIT = ₹120 crore. Change in capital employed = ₹1,200 crore. Incremental ROCE = ₹120 crore ÷ ₹1,200 crore = 10%. Even if the company's reported ROCE still looks respectable at around 15.6% in FY25, every new rupee is earning only 10%, below the cost of capital. The moat is not extending to the new investments.

body.text: Incremental ROCE is where moat erosion shows up first. Reported ROCE is an average of old, protected capital and new, unprotected capital, so it falls slowly and late. Incremental ROCE reveals the problem years earlier.

children.text: Putting It Together: Four Kinds of Business

body.caption: Returns and runway decide what a moat is worth

cells: Compounder: reinvest heavily, earnings grow fast, worth a premium multiple
Cash cow: should pay large dividends or buy back shares; danger is wasteful diversification
Value destroyer: growth consumes capital at returns below the cost of capital; the worst outcome
Harvest: minimal investment, return cash to shareholders, value it as a declining asset

children.text: The most expensive mistake is the bottom left box: a company reinvesting heavily into a large market at poor returns, while its story sounds like the top left. The most common misjudgement is treating a cash cow as a compounder, paying a high multiple for growth the company has no way to deliver.
Category penetration:
many Indian categories, from insurance to organised retail to premium consumer goods, still reach a small share of households. Low penetration with rising incomes is a genuine runway.
Market share headroom:
a company with 8% share of a fragmented market has more room than one with 55% of a mature one.
Geographic expansion:
a regional player moving into new states, provided the moat travels with it. Distribution and brand advantages often do not transfer across regions.
Adjacent products:
extensions that use the same distribution or the same customer trust, which is far safer than entering an unrelated industry.

Be sceptical of total addressable market claims in investor presentations. The relevant question is not how big the market is, but how much of it this company can serve profitably while keeping its moat intact.

body.title: Diagnose the Business
body.question: A listed company has reported ROCE of 26%, pays out 75% of profits as dividends, has grown revenue 5% a year for five years, and operates in a category where it already holds over half the market. What is it, and how should it be valued?
options: A compounder deserving a premium growth multiple
A cash cow: the moat is intact but the runway is short, so value it on its dividend stream and cash generation rather than on growth
body.explanation: High returns with a dominant share and slow growth describe a cash cow. Returning 75% of profit is the right decision, because reinvesting in a saturated category would earn poor returns. The mistake would be paying a compounder multiple, or cheering if management announced a large acquisition in an unrelated industry.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: Reported ROCE blends old and new capital, so moat erosion usually shows up first in ___ ROCE.
body.explanation: Incremental ROCE isolates the return on newly invested capital, which reacts to competitive pressure years before the reported average does.

body.title: The Capex Announcement
body.scenario: A listed branded food company has earned ROCE above 30% for a decade, converts about 95% of profit into operating cash, and runs a negative working capital cycle. It has announced a ₹2,000 crore investment to enter packaged dairy, a category with thin margins, heavy cold chain requirements, and several established competitors. Its existing capital employed is ₹2,500 crore. The stock trades at 55 times earnings.
body.prompt: How should an investor think about this announcement?
body.modelAnswer: The existing business is clearly a moat business: high ROCE, excellent cash conversion, and a negative working capital cycle showing power over suppliers and distributors. The concern is what the new capital will earn. The company is adding almost 80% to its capital employed in one move, into a category with structurally lower margins and higher fixed investment in cold chain. If the new capital earns only 12% to 15%, blended ROCE falls sharply even though nothing is wrong with the original business, and a 55 times multiple assumes continued high-return growth. What to monitor: management's stated return expectations and payback period for the dairy investment; whether the existing brand and distribution genuinely transfer to dairy, which would be the moat travelling with it; incremental ROCE over the next three to five years; cash conversion, since dairy may require more working capital; and whether the company would have created more value by returning the ₹2,000 crore to shareholders. This is precisely the moment when a cash cow can quietly become a value destroyer.

body.label: The three-question cash test
body.value: Does profit become cash, is the cycle short, and does new capital earn moat-level returns?
body.context: A yes to all three, plus a real runway, is what justifies a compounder valuation.

body.title: Run the Cash and Reinvestment Check
steps: On Screener.in, open the Cash Flow section and add up cash from operating activities for the last five years
Add up net profit for the same five years and divide to get cash conversion
Note the cash conversion cycle and its trend in the Ratios section
From the Balance Sheet, calculate capital employed (equity plus borrowings) for the earliest and latest year
Take EBIT for the same two years from the Profit & Loss and calculate incremental ROCE
Check the dividend payout ratio and any recent large capex or acquisition announcements
Place the company in one of the four boxes: compounder, cash cow, value destroyer, or harvest

body.text: All companies and figures in this lesson are hypothetical illustrations. Nothing here is an investment recommendation. Screener.in section names and layouts may change.

points: Compare five-year operating cash flow with five-year net profit; profit rising while cash stays flat is a serious red flag
The cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus debtor days minus payable days, and a negative cycle means the value chain funds the company
Earnings growth equals return on incremental capital times the reinvestment rate
Incremental ROCE, the change in EBIT divided by the change in capital employed, reveals moat erosion years before reported ROCE does
Combine returns with runway: compounder, cash cow, value destroyer, or harvest, and value each differently
The costliest error is paying a compounder multiple for a company reinvesting heavily at poor incremental returns
